item.title: CISA Warns on Exploited SharePoint CVEs as AsyncAPI npm and DriveSurge Campaigns Spread Malware
item.content:encoded:
CISA warns admins to patch actively exploited SharePoint flaws — Must Read

CISA warns that attackers are actively exploiting three on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server flaws to bypass authentication, achieve remote code execution, and steal IIS machine keys for persistence. Admins should urgently apply Microsoft’s latest patches, verify installation, monitor for compromise, and reduce or protect internet exposure.

  • CISA warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, and CVE-2026-56164 to hack internet-exposed on-premises SharePoint Server instances.
  • The three actively exploited vulnerabilities affect all supported self-hosted SharePoint Server versions, including SharePoint Server Subscription Edition.
  • CISA said attackers are using the flaws to bypass authentication, gain remote code execution, steal Internet Information Services machine keys, and gain persistence to deploy malware on compromised systems.
  • Shadowserver tracks nearly 10,000 internet-exposed Microsoft SharePoint servers and more than 800 that are unpatched against CVE-2026-32201 and CVE-2026-45659.
  • CISA recommended applying Microsoft’s latest patches, verifying successful installation, shortening patching cycles, enabling AMSI integration and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detections, and reducing direct internet exposure where possible.

UK Cybercrime Journal: University of Nottingham Breached by ShinyHunters — Must Read

ShinyHunters breached the University of Nottingham and leaked over 40GB of sensitive student, finance, and campus data, including more than 455,000 unique email addresses and highly personal details. The incident is part of a broader campaign targeting education organizations through Oracle PeopleSoft infrastructure using the critical CVE-2026-35273 zero-day.

  • On 9 June 2026, the University of Nottingham was listed as a victim on the ShinyHunters Tor data leak site.
  • ShinyHunters leaked over 40GB of billing and payment records, student finance data, and campus portal exports from the University of Nottingham and its Malaysia and China campuses.
  • Have I Been Pwned analysis found the leaked data contained over 455,000 unique email addresses and personal information including ethnicities, disabilities, and passport numbers.
  • Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group attributed an active compromise and extortion campaign targeting Oracle PeopleSoft infrastructure to UNC6240, also known as ShinyHunters.
  • Google identified over 100 exposed organizations in the Oracle PeopleSoft campaign and noted that 68% were academic institutions, including universities and colleges worldwide.

Compromised AsyncAPI npm Packages Deliver Multi-Stage Botnet Malware — Must Read

Compromised @asyncapi npm packages were used to deliver a multi-stage botnet loader that downloads the Miasma payload from IPFS and can steal credentials, persist, move laterally, and spread through package registries. The attackers abused legitimate GitHub Actions publishing workflows with valid provenance, so affected systems should be treated as potentially compromised if the poisoned modules were loaded.

  • Four compromised npm packages in the @asyncapi namespace were observed distributing a multi-stage botnet loader, affecting @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1, @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, and @asyncapi/specs versions 6.11.2 and 6.11.2-alpha.1.
  • The poisoned packages contained a hidden JavaScript implant that executed when the infected module was loaded by Node.js, not through npm install hooks.
  • The implant downloaded an encrypted second-stage JavaScript loader named sync.js from IPFS, which decoded to the Miasma tasking framework.
  • The Miasma framework supported six command-and-control communication channels: HTTP, Nostr relay, IPFS, BitTorrent DHT, libp2p GossipSub, and an Ethereum smart contract.
  • StepSecurity said the attacker gained push access to repositories and used legitimate GitHub Actions release workflows to publish the packages with valid OIDC provenance attestations, rather than stealing an npm token.

DriveSurge actor uses ClickFix and FakeUpdates to distribute malware via compromised websites — Should Read

The DriveSurge threat actor is compromising websites and using ClickFix social-engineering prompts alongside FakeUpdates lures to deliver malware. The key takeaway is that users should be wary of browser update or fix prompts on websites, as they may be part of an active malware distribution campaign.

  • The article reports that a threat actor named DriveSurge is distributing malware.
  • DriveSurge is using ClickFix as part of the malware distribution activity.
  • DriveSurge is also using FakeUpdates to distribute malware through compromised websites.
  • The malware distribution described in the article involves websites that have been compromised.

US charges alleged operators of Russian bulletproof hosting service — Should Read

U.S. prosecutors charged three Russian nationals accused of running the Media Land and ML.Cloud bulletproof hosting services, which allegedly supported ransomware and cybercrime operations causing over $62 million in damages. The U.S. is also offering up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates or use of the companies.

  • U.S. federal prosecutors unsealed charges against three Russian nationals accused of providing bulletproof hosting services to ransomware gangs that caused over $62 million in damages worldwide.
  • The indictment says Aleksandr Volosovik owned Media Land, Yulia Pankova owned ML Cloud and assisted with legal and financial matters, and Kirill Zatolokin collected customer payments.
  • Media Land and ML.Cloud allegedly provided infrastructure in multiple countries outside Russia, including China, Finland, the Netherlands, and the United States.
  • The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward of up to $10 million for information on foreign government-linked associates of the defendants, their malicious cyber activities, or foreign government-linked use of the companies.
  • The United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia previously sanctioned the three defendants and two companies for providing attack infrastructure and technical support to operations including LockBit, Blacksuit, and Play.

Meta, Microsoft, DOJ, and Others Disrupt Southeast Asia Scam Compounds — Should Read

Meta, Microsoft, the U.S. Department of Justice, and partners coordinated actions to disrupt Southeast Asia-based scam compounds that run large-scale online fraud operations. The key takeaway is that major tech platforms and law enforcement are increasingly targeting the infrastructure and accounts enabling these transnational scams.

  • The article reports that Meta, Microsoft, the DOJ, and others disrupted scam compounds.
  • The disrupted scam compounds were located in Southeast Asia.
  • The article identifies Meta, Microsoft, and the DOJ as participants in the disruption effort.

Over 1.4 Million Accounts Disrupted in Cybercrime Crackdown — Should Read

An international cybercrime crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million malicious accounts, highlighting the scale of coordinated efforts to dismantle online fraud and account-abuse infrastructure.

  • The article reports on a cybercrime crackdown.
  • The crackdown disrupted more than 1.4 million accounts.
  • The disruption of accounts is presented as the central outcome of the crackdown.

Microsoft: Some Dell PCs shut down after recent Windows updates — May Read

Microsoft is temporarily blocking the KB5101650 Windows 11 security update on some Dell PCs after an Intel driver incompatibility caused shutdowns, overheating, poor performance, and battery drain. A fix is being developed with Dell and is expected soon.

  • Microsoft is blocking the KB5101650 Windows 11 security update on some Dell devices because it can cause shutdowns and performance issues.
  • The issue affects a limited number of Dell systems after installing the KB5101650 cumulative update for Windows 11 25H2 and 24H2 devices.
  • Microsoft said the root cause is a conflict between the new Windows USB-C Connection Manager interface introduced in the KB5095093 preview update and the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.
  • Affected devices may show a yellow exclamation point in Device Manager next to the Intel Innovation Platform Framework Processor Participant driver.
  • Microsoft is working with Dell on a fix and plans to release a resolution for affected devices in the coming days.

ADPathFinder: OpenGraph Attack Path Mapping in BloodHound CE — Optional

NetSPI released ADPathFinder, a tool that uses BloodHound CE graph data to automatically find and group privilege escalation paths across AD, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM. It also enriches password audit results with BloodHound context so cracked or weak credentials can be prioritized by real attack-path risk.

  • ADPathFinder maps privilege escalation paths across Active Directory, ADCS, MSSQL, and SCCM using BloodHound graph data.
  • The tool combines SharpHound data with OpenGraph collector data from tools such as MSSQLHound and ConfigManBearPig so cross-dataset paths appear as one finding.
  • ADPathFinder groups users and computers that reach the same target through the same chain, reducing duplicate findings in large environments.
  • The tool can run password audits using NTDS dumps and hashcat potfiles, adding BloodHound context such as group membership, roastability, delegation, and account risk.
  • ADPathFinder generates per-domain HTML reports, along with text and JSON outputs, containing severity-organized findings, attack path graphs, and PowerShell commands to confirm each step.
